title: Nutrition Q&A #1
summary: In his first nutrition Q&A, NH admits nutrition is his weakest area and argues it matters least once your base is set. He eats 120-140 g protein at 95 kg on a high-carb, low-fat diet, says huge protein targets are unnecessary for naturals, explains building muscle in a deficit, and advises non-competitors to judge by the mirror and raise calories slowly.
claims: NH says nutrition is the area where he has done the least research and is least accurate, so take his advice with a grain of salt
The '70-80% nutrition' idea is bogus; nutrition is the least important factor because training takes effort and eating doesn't
Once your nutritional base is built, diet becomes an automatism; a diet shouldn't be a struggle, your training should
Never boil or steam chicken; cook it in the oven or a pan and season heavily so you can eat it in large amounts
NH spent a year eating only chicken breast, spinach, rice and green olives, with occasional dark chocolate
Diversify protein sources: fish, fatty fish and plant proteins, which complement animal proteins
Animal protein is very satiating for its calories, so skinny lifters on high-protein diets fill up and fail to eat enough calories
Beginners with little muscle can't use large amounts of protein; the excess is used as fuel or wasted
For gaining mass total calories matter more than macros; eat carbs even if protein drops, because they are easy to eat and not filling
Eating 2 g/kg protein is unnecessary for most people; past a point protein is burned as fuel, and mainly steroid users can use that much
Anabolism is driven mainly by training, which raises the body's demands, not by extra protein
At 95 kg (210 lb) NH eats about 120-140 g protein a day, 140 only on heavy days, with low fat, moderate protein and high carbs
People pushing high protein are often sponsored by supplement companies that want you to finish the tub quickly
Rule of thumb for supplements: take half the dose the label recommends
Skinny-fat people should stay at maintenance or a very slight surplus or deficit and train for a long time; heavy cuts or bulks teach the body to store fat
NH firmly opposes extreme diets such as keto, zero fat, carnivore or vegan; they suit only a small minority, and humans are omnivores who need a balanced diet
Body fat tests are mostly inaccurate and easy to cheat; track strength and tonnage progression instead as a sign of muscle gain past the novice phase
You can build muscle in a deficit, but slower than at maintenance, which is itself slower than in a surplus
The body prioritises keeping organs alive; in deficit it may shed muscle because muscle burns calories while giving little energy back
Fat is easy for the body to store and costs no energy to maintain, unlike muscle
Any surplus energy the body can't turn into muscle is stored as fat; a perfect lean-gain balance is theoretically possible but can't realistically be tracked
Advanced lifters stop growing or lose muscle in a deficit mainly because they get weaker and can no longer produce the stimulus they're used to
How long results take doesn't matter; it isn't a race, you'll train for the rest of your life
Natural competitors must get to about 10% body fat; below about 8% you start sacrificing so much mass you may not look like you lift
If you don't compete, avoid extreme beach cuts and dysmorphia-driven winter bulks; train smart near maintenance and judge by the mirror, not the scale
There's no formula for optimal weight by height; at higher bodyweight a 2% body fat change is far more fat and looks dramatically different
Your optimal weight is the one that lets you progress in strength and tonnage right now
At 140 lb NH never imagined reaching 210 lb with abs
Maintenance calorie needs rise very slowly unless activity or climate changes; your appetite usually signals it
Raise calories in small steps; adding 300-400 kcal is already a bulk, and a 200 kcal snack on a 2000 kcal diet is a 10% increase
When raising calories, raise protein far more slowly, roughly 1 g protein per 100 kcal, to avoid excessive satiety
viewer_questions: how much protein do you eat, 1 g/lb or 2 g/kg
building muscle in a deficit as skinny-fat and how long it takes
optimal bodyweight to maintain without competing
when to increase protein and calories at maintenance
